topic: AI coding agents: is the model or the harness the bottleneck?

timings.speaker: A
timings.text: Everyone argues whether Claude or GPT is better. But I think you're underrating the harness around them.

timings.speaker: B
timings.text: Exactly. The model sets a ceiling; the harness decides how much of that ceiling you actually get.

timings.speaker: A
timings.text: So your experiment fixed one model and swapped out four different harnesses on twelve Python tasks?

timings.speaker: B
timings.text: Yes. We used EmptyOS, Aider, Goose, Codex, plus Claude Code. Every task was checked by a deterministic verifier.

timings.speaker: A
timings.text: And the results were dramatic: 12 of 12 for your harness versus seven to eight for the others?

timings.speaker: B
timings.text: Right. On easy tasks like fixing a typo, nearly everything passed. The gaps opened on structured work.

timings.speaker: A
timings.text: Like multi-file refactors or deleting a function and fixing every caller?

timings.speaker: B
timings.text: Precisely. EmptyOS flagged broken callers after deletion, then recovered from the resulting errors automatically.

timings.speaker: A
timings.text: Can you show me how a thin harness fails versus yours on that same delete task?

timings.speaker: B
timings.text: If I just remove the function, it breaks imports. My loop notices and fixes; others stop at failure.

timings.speaker: A
timings.text: What about that decoy task where Codex swapped 'hello' for 'goodbye'? Did other harnesses fail too?

timings.speaker: B
timings.text: Yes. Goose failed due to shell quoting issues, while others latched onto the wrong string entirely.

timings.speaker: A
timings.text: So even a smart model can fail if the harness hands it the wrong tools or loop?

timings.speaker: B
timings.text: Absolutely. A perfect model still fails with bad wiring, incorrect formats, or impossible constraints.

timings.speaker: A
timings.text: You also found that the same harness behaved differently depending on which model was underneath it?

timings.speaker: B
timings.text: That surprised me. Aider failed on one model because its tool format wasn't compatible with another.

timings.speaker: A
timings.text: So a good harness makes the model swappable, but only if they can actually talk to each other?

timings.speaker: B
timings.text: Exactly. A heavy harness like EmptyOS bought persistence for stubborn tasks; thinner ones were brittle.

timings.speaker: A
timings.text: Efficiency-wise, how did it compare? You mentioned Claude Code took twice as many iterations?

timings.speaker: B
timings.text: Yes. EmptyOS finished in 49; Claude Code needed 102 round-trips for the same result.

timings.speaker: A
timings.text: But your local free model did well too, right? Did it miss anything big?

timings.speaker: B
timings.text: It missed a fifteen-file refactor where frontier models' stubbornness paid off. Persistence wins on nastiest tasks.

timings.speaker: A
timings.text: You admitted your first results were wrong because you built the test yourself?

timings.speaker: B
timings.text: I did. I blamed others for my setup errors, like not giving Aider its files or misreading config flags.

timings.speaker: A
timings.text: So you almost published a table that flattered your own system before the audits stopped it?

timings.speaker: B
timings.text: Yes. Once I checked those flags and re-run things, the true picture emerged.
